III def3 p132.text:
By emotion I mean the modifications of the body, whereby the active power of the said body is increased or diminished, aided or constrained, and also the ideas of such modifications.

N.B. If we can be the adequate cause of any of these modifications, I then call the emotion an activity, otherwise I call it a passion, or state wherein the mind is passive.
III def3 p132.alignment: Latin p. 132 definition III and both English sentences correspond in full: Affectum becomes emotion, affectiones modifications, power increases or decreases and is aided or constrained; the N.B. heading and the explication of passion as a passive state of mind are features of Elwes, not explicit words in the Latin.

III affects2 p184.text: Pleasure is the transition of a man from a less to a greater perfection.
III affects2 p184.alignment: Latin p. 184 definition II Laetitia is rendered Pleasure by Elwes; both state transition from lesser to greater perfection. Pleasure is this historical translator’s term, not a claim that Laetitia means only sensory pleasure.

III affects3 p184.text: Pain is the transition of a man from a greater to a less perfection.
III affects3 p184.alignment: Latin p. 184 definition III Tristitia is rendered Pain by Elwes; both state transition from greater to lesser perfection. Pain is this historical translator’s term, not a claim that Tristitia means only physical pain.

III def3 p132.alignment: Personally read Latin Paulus p. 132 and Elwes 1891 p. 130: both full sentences align, including the adequate cause and action/passion distinction; Elwes adds the N.B. label and explanatory words about the mind being passive. Emotion renders affectus, modifications renders affectiones. The English wording matches the printed page, with print emphasis removed.

III affects2 p184.alignment: Personally read Latin Paulus p. 184 definition II and Elwes 1891 p. 174: both specify a human transition from lesser to greater perfection. The English sentence matches the printed page; pleasure is Elwes’s rendering of laetitia, not a restriction to sensory pleasure.

III affects3 p184.alignment: Personally read Latin Paulus p. 184 definition III and Elwes 1891 p. 174: both specify a human transition from greater to lesser perfection. The English sentence matches the printed page; pain is Elwes’s rendering of tristitia, not a restriction to physical pain.
